limits.description: Article 75 of the Convention Implementing the Schengen Agreement (CISA) lets travelers carry 'the narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances that are necessary for their medical treatment' if, at any check, they can produce a certificate issued or authenticated by a competent authority of their state of residence. Article 75 itself leaves the certificate's exact form and the details on permitted quantity and journey duration to the Schengen Executive Committee; in practice the resulting 'Schengen certificate' is understood to cover only the quantity needed for a journey of up to 30 days.
limits.quantity: up to a 30-day supply, evidenced by the Schengen certificate

notes: This is a Schengen-wide legal basis (confirmed directly from Article 75's text), but the certificate itself is issued nationally — by a doctor, pharmacist, or health authority depending on the member state — before you travel; there is no single EU-wide online portal. Article 75 covers 'narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances' as legal classes rather than naming individual medicines, but these classes are the internationally scheduled categories (1961 and 1971 UN conventions) that cover common stimulants (Adderall/amphetamine, Vyvanse/lisdexamfetamine, Ritalin/methylphenidate), benzodiazepines (Xanax/alprazolam, Valium/diazepam, Klonopin/clonazepam), and opioid painkillers (codeine, oxycodone, tramadol). Some Schengen states still restrict or ban specific substances outright under their own national law regardless of the certificate — for example, the UK's own guidance (a non-Schengen state, cited here only as an illustration of the pattern) notes a Schengen certificate cannot be used to bring a Schedule 1 drug into Great Britain. Confirm with the specific member state's narcotics authority before traveling with an unusual medication.

legal_source.name: Convention Implementing the Schengen Agreement, Art. 75

limits.description: Kenya Revenue Authority's traveler FAQ lists 'Narcotic drugs' among goods prohibited for import outright (citing the 2nd and 3rd Schedule of the East African Community Customs Management Act), while listing 'Medicaments' generally among restricted goods that may be imported once 'authorization by relevant Government Institutions' is obtained. notes: This is a genuine, unresolved gap in KRA's public guidance, not a confirmed 'allowed' or 'banned' answer. Kenya's controlling law for scheduled drugs is the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (Control) Act, 1994, and the Pharmacy and Poisons Board is Kenya's medicines regulator, but no traveler-facing page from either body could be reached in this pass (pharmacyboardkenya.org returned an expired-certificate error; NACADA's site had no relevant guidance) to confirm whether a foreign prescription is sufficient or a specific permit is required. Anyone carrying an ADHD stimulant, benzodiazepine, or opioid painkiller should contact a Kenyan diplomatic mission or the Pharmacy and Poisons Board before travel rather than assume the ordinary prescription-medication allowance covers it.

notes: South Africa separately schedules narcotics/psychotropics under the Medicines and Related Substances Act (Schedules 5 and 6) and the Drugs and Drug Trafficking Act, administered by SAHPRA and SAPS respectively, but no SAHPRA or SAPS page addressing a traveler's personal-use import of scheduled substances could be reached in this pass — SAHPRA's public import-permit pages (importation-of-medical-products-border-control) describe commercial/institutional importation processes, not personal baggage. Given SARS's own guide leaves the 'habit-forming drug' vs 'personal medicine' classification unresolved for controlled prescription drugs, travelers carrying stimulants, benzodiazepines, or opioid painkillers should carry the original prescription plus a doctor's letter and confirm status with SAHPRA or a South African diplomatic mission before travel.

Under Mexico's Ley General de Salud, 'sustancias psicotrópicas' is the class that covers common controlled stimulants (e.g. amphetamine/Adderall, methylphenidate/Ritalin, lisdexamfetamine/Vyvanse) and benzodiazepines (e.g. alprazolam/Xanax, diazepam/Valium, clonazepam/Klonopin), so a doctor's prescription for these should be sufficient for personal-use quantities at the border.

notes: ANAM's traveler-facing text names only 'sustancias psicotrópicas' (psychotropic substances) — it does not mention 'estupefacientes' (narcotic drugs), the separate Mexican legal category that covers opioid painkillers such as codeine, oxycodone, and tramadol. Whether the same simple prescription-only rule extends to opioid painkillers, or whether they instead require the more formal COFEPRIS sanitary import permit used for controlled narcotics (Permiso Sanitario COFEPRIS-03-023, aimed primarily at commercial/institutional importers), is not addressed by ANAM's page, so opioid painkillers are deliberately left out of this entry's name list. No numeric day-supply or unit-quantity cap is published for psychotropics either. Travelers carrying opioid painkillers should confirm with COFEPRIS (tel. 800 033 5050) or a Mexican consulate before travel.

Carry the medication in original packaging with your prescription or a doctor's letter, and declare injector pens/needles if asked.

notes: The Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) — which took over the Ministry of Health and Prevention's (MOHAP) controlled-medicines functions on 29 Dec 2025 under Federal Decree-Law No. 38 of 2024 — offers an optional electronic pre-approval permit before travel; it is NOT strictly mandatory, and travelers may instead simply declare the medicine with prescription + medical report at the port of entry. In practice, undeclared or undocumented controlled medication is what has led to detentions at UAE airports historically, even for drugs that are technically allowed with paperwork — this row corrects the common assumption (from older secondary press reporting) that these drugs are outright banned; per EDE's own current list they are not, but the documentation bar (prescription AND medical report, not just prescription alone) is stricter than most countries. This list is dated 15/09/2022 by EDE/MOHAP but remains the current published schedule as of Sept 2026; it explicitly states non-inclusion of a substance doesn't mean it's uncontrolled, so travelers with any other controlled medication should verify against EDE directly. notes: This is Brazil's general 'accompanied baggage' rule and applies to ordinary prescription and OTC medicines, biologics, and medical products alike. limits.description: Whether a controlled medicine can be imported depends on which of ANVISA's schedules (Lists A1, A2, A3, B1, B2, C1–C5, set by Portaria SVS/MS n° 344/1998) its active substance is on. Medicines on List C1 may be brought in with only a valid medical prescription shown to the sanitary authority at the port of entry — no advance ANVISA authorization is needed, provided no similar product is registered/sold in Brazil (commercial sale of the imported product is prohibited; personal use only). Medicines on Lists A1, A2, A3, B1, B2, C2 and C5 cannot be imported by a traveler at all without ANVISA's advance, case-by-case 'exceptional use' authorization: the patient/legal guardian must petition before travel through ANVISA's SEI electronic system with a signed prescription (patient name, commercial drug name, dosage, quantity, treatment duration, doctor's signature/CRM), a medical report (diagnosis/CID, case history, justification vs. Brazilian-registered alternatives), and a signed liability statement. Approval is not guaranteed and, once granted, must be presented at the ANVISA airport post to release the medicine.

notes: Substances on List C3 (teratogenic/immunosuppressant, e.g. thalidomide, lenalidomide, pomalidomide) are excluded even from the exceptional-use pathway. Substances on Lists E and F are proscribed outright — import, export, trade and use are illegal for any purpose other than authorized research. This pass verified the mechanism directly from ANVISA's official 'Importação de produtos controlados' page, but did not cross-check the live substance-by-substance annex (Portaria 344/1998, Anexo I, which is amended periodically by separate RDCs) to confirm exactly which list captures each named drug — e.g. whether Adderall/amphetamine, Xanax/alprazolam, Valium/diazepam, Klonopin/clonazepam, codeine, oxycodone or tramadol individually sit on C1 versus one of the prohibited-without-authorization lists. Confirm your specific medicine's list before travel via ANVISA's published substance list or its helpline (0800 642 9782).

Products 'that require direct oversight or administration by a trained operator' additionally require the importer to provide the contact details of the Rwandan health facility/provider who will administer them — self-injected insulin/GLP-1 pens would not normally fall in that category, but this was not explicitly confirmed for these specific products.

limits.description: Individuals may cross the U.S. border with a Schedule II-V controlled substance for personal medical use if (1) it is in the original container it was dispensed in, and (2) the traveler declares it to a CBP officer, stating either the trade/chemical name and schedule, or the prescribing practitioner/pharmacy and prescription number. U.S. residents bringing such medication back into the U.S. after obtaining it abroad are capped at 50 dosage units combined across all such medication; that cap does not apply to medication lawfully obtained in the U.S. before departure, and the source does not state it applying to non-resident visitors entering with their own foreign prescription.
limits.quantity: 50 dosage units (U.S. residents only, for meds obtained abroad)

notes: This is a DEA regulation (21 CFR 1301.26), separate from CBP's 90-day-supply guidance on the site's general 'prescription medication' entry -- the two operate together. By DEA scheduling (a well-established, separately-documented fact, not itself re-verified against a DEA scheduling page in this pass), Schedule II covers amphetamine/Adderall, methylphenidate/Ritalin, lisdexamfetamine/Vyvanse and oxycodone; Schedule IV covers alprazolam/Xanax, diazepam/Valium, clonazepam/Klonopin and tramadol; codeine spans Schedule II-V depending on formulation -- all fall within the II-V range this exemption covers. The regulation text itself does not name these drugs by brand, only by schedule.

legal_source.name: U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration / eCFR -- 21 CFR 1301.26, Exemption of certain persons from registration for personal use of controlled substances

limits.description: As FDA-approved prescription drugs, GLP-1 medications (semaglutide/tirzepatide) and insulin follow the FDA's personal importation framework: foreign visitors may bring in roughly a 90-day supply, with the prescription or a doctor's letter. Separately, at TSA airport security screening, insulin is confirmed as a permitted 'medically necessary liquid' in carry-on above the standard 3.4oz limit -- travelers must tell the officer and place it in a bin separately for X-ray screening; the final decision rests with the TSA officer.

notes: Compounded or non-FDA-approved semaglutide/tirzepatide products are treated differently: FDA's personal importation policy only extends discretionary allowance to unapproved drugs when there's a serious condition, no domestic availability, no unreasonable risk, and written affirmation of personal use. Genuine brand-name Ozempic/Wegovy/Mounjaro/Zepbound are FDA-approved, so this stricter unapproved-drug pathway shouldn't apply to them, but a compounded version should expect more scrutiny. The TSA insulin page (https://www.tsa.gov/travel/security-screening/whatcanibring/items/insulin, checked 2026-09-13) doesn't separately name GLP-1 pens, syringes specifically, or give refrigeration/ice-pack rules -- a dedicated TSA syringes/needles/ice-pack page could not be located in this pass, so treat 'same handling as insulin' as a reasonable inference rather than a directly confirmed rule.

legal_source.name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration -- Personal Importation of Drugs

limits.description: Up to 3 months' supply of medicine containing a controlled drug can be carried in hand luggage without a Home Office licence. All of the stimulants, benzodiazepines and opioids named in this entry are Schedule 2-4 drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations (amphetamine, methylphenidate and lisdexamfetamine: Schedule 2; oxycodone: Schedule 2; codeine: Schedule 2 or 5 depending on the preparation; tramadol: Schedule 3; diazepam, alprazolam and clonazepam: Schedule 4 Part 1), so the 3-month exemption applies to them -- only Schedule 1 drugs are barred without a special licence. Non-UK residents must carry a letter stating their name, travel dates, and a list of the medicine with dose/strength, signed by the prescriber; the medicine must travel in hand luggage, not hold luggage.

notes: UK residents needing more than 3 months, or anyone needing a Schedule 1 drug, must apply in advance to the Home Office's Drugs and Firearms Licensing Unit (DFLU) -- the source doesn't give a lead time for this specific case (a different gov.uk page about importing/exporting controlled drugs generally recommends applying at least 14 days ahead, which is what the site's general prescription-medication-gb entry cites). None of Adderall/Xanax/Valium/Klonopin/codeine/oxycodone/tramadol are Schedule 1 in the UK, so an outright ban shouldn't apply to them at ordinary personal-use quantities.

legal_source.name: gov.uk -- Taking controlled drugs into the UK

limits.description: Liquid medication over 100ml (which covers most injectable pens/vials) is allowed through UK airport security in hand luggage, but you must carry proof it's prescribed to you -- a prescription copy or a letter from your doctor. Hypodermic syringes are explicitly listed as permitted in hand luggage. No such proof is required for tablets or for liquid medicine in containers of 100ml or less.

notes: Cooling gel packs to keep injectable medication cold are allowed in both hand and hold luggage; ice packs specifically require contacting the airport in advance, per this same gov.uk page. This is UK airport-security screening guidance rather than a customs-import statute, but it's the primary UK government source found for the needle/cold-chain mechanics of carrying GLP-1s and insulin. It does not name Ozempic/Wegovy/Mounjaro or GLP-1 drugs by brand -- insulin and injectable medicines are covered only as a general liquid-medication category.

legal_source.name: gov.uk -- Hand luggage restrictions: essential medicines and medical equipment

limits.description: Under CBSA's Section 56 Class Exemption, travelers may personally carry (in person only -- not by mail or courier) a prescribed narcotic or Food and Drug Regulations Part G controlled drug up to the lesser of a single course of treatment or a 30-day supply, and a prescribed benzodiazepine/targeted substance up to the lesser of a single course of treatment or a 90-day supply. Opioids (codeine, oxycodone, tramadol) and stimulants (amphetamine, methylphenidate/Ritalin, lisdexamfetamine/Vyvanse) fall under the narcotic/Part-G 30-day limit; benzodiazepines (diazepam/Valium, alprazolam/Xanax, clonazepam/Klonopin) get the 90-day limit. Medication must be in pharmacy- or hospital-dispensed packaging with proper labelling, and must be declared to a CBSA officer at the border.

notes: No advance import permit is required for these amounts under the Class Exemption -- but it does not cover Annex I-listed substances unless separately approved by Health Canada or the source country's regulator, and it explicitly does not apply to shipping controlled substances by mail or courier, only carrying them in person.

legal_source.name: Canada Border Services Agency -- Memorandum D19-9-2, Importation and Exportation of Controlled Substances and Precursors

limits.description: GLP-1 drugs and insulin are ordinary (non-controlled) prescription drugs in Canada, so the general personal-use rule applies: a single course of treatment or a 90-day supply, whichever is less, hand-carried in original/clearly labelled pharmacy packaging. Health Canada's guidance separately states that medical devices imported for personal use -- which covers self-administered injection pens, syringes and needles -- are not restricted under the Food and Drugs Act or Medical Devices Regulations, provided the device doesn't require a trained operator, i.e. it's meant for the patient's own self-administration.

notes: This guidance document does not mention insulin, GLP-1 drugs, needles or syringes by name -- the 90-day rule is the same generic prescription-drug provision already used for the site's general prescription-medication-ca entry, and the needle/syringe treatment is inferred from the document's general 'medical devices for personal use' section, not a dedicated sharps policy. No refrigeration/cold-chain guidance was found on this source.

legal_source.name: Health Canada -- Personal Use Health Products Guidance

limits.description: Australia's traveller's exemption lets you bring up to 3 months' supply of your prescription medicine, and the Office of Drug Control confirms this covers Schedule 8-type medicines too: 'Prescription medicines such as morphine, oxycodone, methadone, methylphenidate, Adderall, and benzodiazepines are all covered by the traveller exemption.' Codeine-containing medication is also covered but 'requires a prescription from your medical doctor.' You need a valid prescription or a doctor's letter stating the medicine name and dosage, and the medicine should stay in its original packaging with the dispensing label intact; declare everything to the Australian Border Force on arrival.

notes: If you need more than 3 months' worth, ODC's guidance points to either getting a new prescription from an Australian-registered prescriber, or importing a further 3-month supply if the medicine isn't otherwise restricted -- it does not describe an advance import-permit process for a longer personal supply of these particular drugs, unlike Thailand's or Japan's schemes. Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is not named individually on this source (only 'methylphenidate' and 'Adderall' are used as the stimulant examples) and so is omitted from this entry's names, even though it is a similar stimulant class. Methadone is also named as covered by the source but isn't included here since it wasn't part of the requested drug list.

legal_source.name: Australian Government Office of Drug Control -- Travelling to Australia with medicines and medical devices

limits.description: Insulin and other injectable medicines fall under the same traveller's exemption as other prescription medicines: bring up to 3 months' supply, carry your prescription or a doctor's letter naming the medicine and dose, keep it in original packaging, and declare it to the Australian Border Force. TGA's own traveller guidance uses an insulin worked example: a diabetic traveller kept insulin in its original packaging with a prescription and doctor's letter, and used a small cooler bag on board to keep it cold during a long-haul flight.

notes: Neither the TGA nor ODC pages fetched in this pass name GLP-1 drugs (Ozempic/Wegovy/Mounjaro/Zepbound, semaglutide/tirzepatide) specifically, or address needles/syringes/injection pens as their own category -- they're covered only by extension as ordinary prescription medicines/medical devices under the general traveller's exemption, and by the insulin example for cold-chain handling. If you need more than 3 months' supply, the same 'get a local prescription or import a further batch' guidance from the general controlled-medicine entry applies.

legal_source.name: Therapeutic Goods Administration -- Entering Australia (travelling with medicines and medical devices)

limits.description: Medicines that are controlled drugs under New Zealand's Misuse of Drugs Act must be declared on the New Zealand Traveller Declaration and are capped at one month's supply (versus three months for ordinary prescription medicines), carried in original packaging with a prescription copy or a doctor's letter confirming the treatment.

notes: Neither NZ Customs' nor Medsafe's traveller pages (as fetched in this pass) name which specific drugs count as 'controlled drugs' for this rule -- there's no breakdown by stimulant/benzodiazepine/opioid class or schedule number, unlike Thailand's or Canada's guidance for the same topic. Under NZ's Misuse of Drugs Act, amphetamine-type stimulants, benzodiazepines (diazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam) and many opioids (codeine above OTC strength, oxycodone, tramadol) are classified as controlled drugs, but that classification was not independently confirmed against a primary NZ legal source in this pass -- the Ministry of Health's controlled-drugs page returned an access error (403) when fetched. Verdict is marked 'depends' rather than 'allowed_with_limits' for that reason. Adderall and Vyvanse specifically were not checked and are omitted; treat their NZ status as unconfirmed.

legal_source.name: New Zealand Customs Service -- Prohibited and restricted items: medicines

notes: NZ Customs' prohibited-and-restricted-items page explicitly bans 'cannabis utensils' (bongs, vaporisers, hash pipes) as drug paraphernalia, and does not list cannabis or CBD anywhere among the medicines a traveller may bring under the ordinary prescription-medicine or controlled-drugs provisions (which are capped at 3 months' and 1 month's supply respectively, with no cannabis-specific carve-out named). New Zealand's 2020 cannabis-legalisation referendum failed, so recreational cannabis remains illegal; Medsafe's own site (medsafe.govt.nz) was checked in this pass and surfaced no traveller-facing guidance on medicinal cannabis import either. Treat any cannabis or CBD product, including hemp-derived, as prohibited for personal import absent a specific NZ medicinal-cannabis import authorisation obtained in advance.

legal_source.name: New Zealand Customs Service -- Prohibited and restricted items

limits.description: "All firearms, weapons and ammunition are prohibited in New Zealand without a permit." Authorisation must be obtained from Te Tari Pūreke — Firearms Safety Authority (FSA) or New Zealand Police before travelling with firearms, weapons, ammunition, or firearm parts. The same permit requirement covers airguns, stun devices, pepper spray, and various knife types — none of these can simply be declared and allowed through; a permit obtained in advance is required.

notes: NZ Customs places the burden of verifying permit requirements on the traveller or importer before arrival — there is no on-arrival process to obtain a permit you didn't already have. Ordinary pocket/kitchen knives packed in checked luggage are typically a separate, lower-risk case in practice, but the source's own wording sets a wide 'various knife types' net without a clear-cut personal-use exemption, so travellers should not assume any knife is automatically fine.

legal_source.name: New Zealand Customs Service — Prohibited and restricted items

limits.description: "Some plants and animals are protected under international law. This includes items made from endangered species. You must not bring these items into New Zealand without the correct permits." NZ Customs names corals, clams, crocodile products, and certain traditional medicines as commonly seized items; the Department of Conservation issues permits (where obtainable at all) for ivory products, animal skins, leather goods, furs, shells, marine life items, protected timber, and live species.

notes: This is a CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species) enforcement matter, not a simple customs allowance — many categories named here (ivory in particular) have no realistic personal-import permit path even when a permit process technically exists. Souvenirs bought abroad (coral jewellery, tortoiseshell items, animal-skin goods) are a common, easy-to-miss trap for travellers who assume a small souvenir quantity is exempt; the source states no such exemption. Anyone uncertain should contact the Department of Conservation (cites@doc.govt.nz) before travel, not after purchasing the item.

legal_source.name: New Zealand Customs Service — Prohibited and restricted items

limits.description: Saudi Arabia's SFDA-run Controlled Drugs System (CDS) traveler-clearance regime applies only to medicines containing narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances (see the separate controlled-medication entry) — the SFDA's published traveler clearance terms do not describe a separate permit or state a numeric quantity cap for ordinary (non-controlled) prescription or OTC medicine.
limits.quantity: No published numeric limit found; bring only a reasonable personal-use quantity.

notes: Bring medicine in its original, labeled packaging and carry a copy of the prescription or a doctor's letter for prescription items. SFDA has not published a specific personal-use quantity limit (e.g. a days'-supply cap) for non-controlled medicines that could be independently confirmed in this research; only medicines classified as narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances require the advance CDS clearance permit described in the controlled-medication entry.

legal_source.name: Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) — Controlled Drugs System (CDS), User Manual for Traveler Clearance (defines the scope of the traveler permit regime as narcotic drugs/psychotropic substances only)

limits.description: Any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance carried by a traveler for personal treatment (the kind of medicine that, as commonly prescribed, includes stimulants such as Adderall/amphetamine and Ritalin/methylphenidate, benzodiazepines such as Xanax/alprazolam and Valium/diazepam, and opioid painkillers such as codeine and oxycodone) must be cleared in advance through SFDA's Controlled Drugs System (CDS) at cds.sfda.gov.sa before arrival in or departure from Saudi Arabia. Clearance requires either (a) a detailed medical report from a licensed medical institution, issued within the last 6 months, naming the diagnosis, treatment plan, and the drug's scientific name and dosage, or (b) a doctor's prescription in the patient's name, issued within the last 6 months, with diagnosis, drug details and the institution's seal — plus a copy of the patient's ID and a signed pledge that the medicine is for the named patient's own use at their own risk.
limits.quantity: No published blanket days'-supply figure; each medicine/quantity is submitted individually through the CDS online request for SFDA approval.

notes: Drugs listed in Category (D) of Schedule I, Category (A) of Schedule II, or Paragraph (IV) of the Psychotropic Substances schedule under Saudi Arabia's Law of Combating Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances cannot be cleared for travelers under any circumstances, regardless of prescription — SFDA's traveler-clearance document does not name which specific brand-name medicines fall in these banned categories, only the schedule references, so travelers should confirm their specific medication's classification with SFDA before applying. Apply through the CDS system before travel; the guidance does not state a fixed processing time.

limits.description: Under Dangerous Drugs Board Regulation No. 1, Series of 2014, Section 35, a traveler entering, leaving, or passing through the Philippines who is under treatment for a medical condition may possess a dangerous drug or a drug preparation containing a controlled chemical, in a quantity reasonable for that treatment, when prescribed by a physician. For a supply of up to 30 days, the traveler must carry: (a) a letter from the attending physician describing the medical condition, (b) the physician's prescription listing the trade and generic names of the drug, and the medicine in its original, properly labeled container — no advance PDEA permit is required for this 30-day case.
limits.quantity: Up to 30 days' supply with physician's letter + prescription only. For a supply exceeding 30 days, the traveler additionally needs Certificates of Authorization from PDEA and from the National Competent Authority of their home country (incoming) or destination country (outgoing); the PDEA request must be submitted in writing at least 30 working days before travel, and PDEA replies within 15 working days.

notes: The regulation governs 'dangerous drugs' and 'drug preparations containing a controlled chemical' generally (as scheduled under RA 9165, the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002) rather than naming specific brands like Adderall or Xanax; it does not itself state which named medicines fall in which schedule. Common stimulants (amphetamine, methylphenidate), benzodiazepines (diazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam) and opioid painkillers (codeine, oxycodone) are the general classes of substance this regime is understood to cover, but travelers should confirm their specific medicine's PH classification with PDEA before travel. Outgoing travelers must also check the destination country's own requirements.

legal_source.name: Philippine Dangerous Drugs Board — Board Regulation No. 1, Series of 2014 (Comprehensive Amendments to Board Regulation No. 3, Series 2003), Section 35: Carrying of Dangerous Drugs and/or Drug Preparation containing Controlled Chemical by International Travelers

notes: RA 9165 (Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002), Sec. 3(j), defines 'Dangerous Drugs' as those listed in the Schedules annexed to the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs (as amended by the 1972 Protocol) and the 1971 Single Convention on Psychotropic Substances — both of which schedule cannabis and its resin. The Board Regulation 1/2014 medical-travel exception cited on this site's 'controlled medication' entry for the Philippines applies to prescribed pharmaceutical drug preparations with a physician's letter and prescription; it does not extend to raw cannabis, marijuana, or unregistered CBD products, which the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) treats as prohibited dangerous drugs with no personal-travel carve-out found on the sources checked in this pass. The Philippines is well known for severe, actively-enforced penalties for dangerous-drugs offences — travelers should not assume any personal-use or small-quantity exception exists.

legal_source.name: Republic Act No. 9165 — Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002, Sec. 3(j) (Dangerous Drugs)

limits.quantity: No specific numeric personal-use quantity cap for ordinary medicine is stated on this page.

It does not give a numeric quantity limit for non-controlled medicine, only that medicines trigger mandatory physical inspection; travelers should carry medicines in original packaging with a prescription/doctor's letter, especially for quantities that could look like more than personal use.

Indonesia is widely known to impose severe penalties for narcotics offences, up to and including capital punishment for trafficking-level quantities — travelers should not assume any personal-use exception exists.

limits.description: Indonesian Customs' passenger-baggage guidance lists 'senjata api' (firearms), 'senjata angin' (air weapons, e.g. air rifles/airsoft) and 'senjata tajam' (sharp weapons) — alongside narcotics and explosives — as categories that trigger mandatory red-lane physical inspection. notes: Bea Cukai's page does not give a numeric size/blade-length threshold for 'senjata tajam,' nor does it name an exception for ordinary pocket knives or multitools packed in checked luggage — travelers carrying anything that could be characterised as a weapon should expect inspection and be ready to justify it, not assume a small size makes it exempt.
